en.title: You Can See Everything Crosses $100M, Cracks Golden Globes' Exclusive Club
en.summary: The unconventional documentary **You Can See Everything** has achieved a stunning box office milestone, surpassing $100 million and potentially earning a coveted spot at the Golden Globes. This financial success bypasses the ceremony's long-standing exclusion of non-scripted films.
en.body:
In a move that’s turning heads and perhaps raising a few eyebrows at the Hollywood Foreign Press Association, the documentary **You Can See Everything** is reportedly on the verge of crossing the $100 million mark at the domestic box office. This incredible financial achievement not only solidifies its place as one of the most profitable documentaries in history but also, crucially, provides a potential backdoor into the prestigious Golden Globe Awards. The Globes have long maintained a strict policy against documentaries competing in their major categories, preferring what they deem "scripted" features. This rule has historically barred non-fiction films, regardless of their artistic merit or narrative complexity.

Directed by **Nathan Fielder** and **Lance Oppenheim**, **You Can See Everything** employs creative filmmaking techniques, including actor recreations, to depict events that weren't captured by the camera. This very approach, while enhancing the storytelling, would typically disqualify it from most Globes categories. However, the film's extraordinary box office performance has opened a door to the Globes' **Best Cinematic And Box Office Achievement** award. According to awards season trackers like Gold Derby, achieving $100 million domestically is a key requirement for a film to qualify for this specific category, which is notably the only one that doesn't explicitly ban documentaries.

## A Box Office Anomaly
The success of **You Can See Everything** is nothing short of remarkable. Against industry trends and often defying box office gravity, the film has resonated deeply with audiences worldwide. It has become A24's third-biggest domestic release ever, a testament to its broad appeal. This financial triumph is particularly significant given the Globes' historical stance. The HFPA's rules have often been criticized for being opaque or even self-serving, with some speculating it's less about artistic purity and more about ensuring star-studded parties rather than candid conversations with documentarians. Whatever the underlying reason, **You Can See Everything**'s financial might is now its most powerful credential.

## What This Means for Fans and the Globes
For fans of **You Can See Everything**, this box office milestone is a validation of their passion and a thrilling development in its awards season journey. It raises the stakes for the Golden Globes, forcing them to either acknowledge a film that has captured the public's imagination through sheer financial success or to double down on their exclusionary policies. This situation tests the Globes' commitment to recognizing cinematic achievement, regardless of genre. It’s a narrative arc many binge-watchers and series fans can appreciate: a story of an underdog, defying the odds and challenging established norms.

## What's Next
With the $100 million threshold reportedly crossed, all eyes will be on the Golden Globe nominations announcement to see if **You Can See Everything** receives a nod in the **Best Cinematic And Box Office Achievement** category. The industry will be watching closely to see how this financial success impacts the HFPA's traditional eligibility interpretations.

content_raw: Of the many quirks (and/or “instances of weirdly insular, occasionally-difficult-to-not-just-label-as-blatantly-corrupt ” behavior) that perpetually afflict the Golden Globes, the award ceremony’s staunch anti-documentary stance is one of the oddest. The Hollywood Foreign Press Association’s eligibility rules for the Globes straight-up disallow documentaries and any other features that aren’t “scripted” from competing in any of the show’s major categories, including Best Picture—either out of some straight-edge celebration of the fictional arts, or the to-our-minds more likely possibility that the HFPA simply didn’t get into this game to hang out at their big party with nerdy documentarians instead of actual movie stars . The upshot is that even docs with some actual writing and performance in them—like, say, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s  You Can See Everything , which makes extensive use of actor recreations to show the audience moments that the pair’s cameras didn’t capture—are barred from competing. Unless, of course, the money’s good. The money has, in fact, turned out to be good, as  You Can See Everything  is reportedly set to cross the $100 million mark at the box office this weekend—not only making it one of the most profitable documentaries in cinematic history, but also giving it a back door into the Globes. This is per awards season obsessives Gold Derby , who note that $100 million domestic is one of the hoops a movie has to jump through in order to qualify for the Globes’ Best Cinematic And Box Office Achievement award, the show’s only category that doesn’t explicitly ban documentaries from competing. (Possibly because no one involved ever expected a doc to March Of The Penguins or Fahrenheit 9/11 its way to those kinds of receipts again.) And while  YCSE  hasn’t yet cleared the $150 million worldwide take that’s also required for the blockbuster-minded award—in part because it still hasn’t released in the vast majority of English-speaking, non-U.S. countries—A24 has reportedly gone ahead and submitted it for a nomination anyway. And while we’re not going to sit here and tell you that the Elizabeth Holmes documentary’s status at Hollywood’s most deliberately frivolous award ceremony is really going to matter much—we do not expect Fielder to overcome, say, Spider-Man , let alone every Avenger under the exploding sun, in the “Movie that made a lot of money” category—the idea of this incredibly weird, deliberately unsettling film competing against, like, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie  does tickle us just a little bit.
